canonical_policy.name: Default validation/logging
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: FluentValidation is the standard explicit request/use-case validation library; application logging uses ILogger<T> with Serilog as provider.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Explicit validator DI integration and ban on legacy auto-validation packages supplement standard FluentValidation; application ILogger remains despite provider-specific edge APIs. Union records each; owning-layer/no-duplication issues reviewed under API/ARC.

context_quotes:
- Default: represent common expected outcomes explicitly when useful (`null`, `bool`, a typed outcome); do not force a generic `Result<T>` pattern, and do not use HTTP-named outcome categories in Application.
- Use FluentValidation for explicit request/use-case validation where appropriate. Validation must stay at its owning boundary: transport/request concerns in Api, use-case and straightforward workflow rules in Application, non-trivial invariants in Domain, assumptions about external systems in Infrastructure when needed; do not duplicate the same rule mechanically at every layer.
- Must not establish business exceptions as the default architecture or throw and catch exceptions merely to jump between normal expected branches.

- Default: `ILogger<T>` with structured message templates and stable property names; avoid string interpolation that turns structured values into opaque text.
- Default: when Serilog is configured, use the DI-integrated `AddSerilog` approach and keep provider configuration in environment-aware configuration; application code continues to depend on `ILogger<T>`.

With `[ApiController]`, ASP.NET Core handles model-binding failures and produces validation problem responses. FluentValidation expresses explicit rules: required business/application input, string or collection constraints, ranges, cross-property and conditional validation.

```text
API transport/request-contract concern        -> API boundary validation
Application use-case input / workflow rule    -> Application validator or Application Service
Non-trivial invariant genuinely owned by Domain -> Domain model
```

Do not move Domain invariants into FluentValidation merely because the library is available, and do not duplicate one rule in several layers unless each has a distinct reason. Register validators with `FluentValidation.DependencyInjectionExtensions`; do not add deprecated/legacy ASP.NET automatic-validation integration packages, and follow the project's established invocation pattern instead of adding a competing one. A syntactically valid request can still violate an Application or Domain rule.

Returning raw exception messages, inconsistent anonymous error objects, putting business rules only in request validators, and coupling validation to Minimal API endpoint filters when Controllers are the HTTP model.

| Scenario | Default |

| Invalid HTTP input | Validation problem response |

Keep test data explicit and minimal. Introduce builders, fixtures, or factories when repeated setup becomes hard to read; do not add a generic test-data framework for a few simple objects.

## Naming

`MethodOrScenario_StateOrCondition_ExpectedBehavior`, for example `CreateOrder_WithValidRequest_ReturnsCreated`, `CreateOrder_WithMissingCustomer_ReturnsValidationError`, `GetOrder_WithUnknownId_ReturnsNotFound`. Follow an established project convention when one exists.

## Regression tests and probe conversion

A regression test reproduces the failure before the fix and passes after it; skip it when the problem cannot realistically recur or is already covered. Convert temporary behavioral checks — ad-hoc HTTP/curl/PowerShell requests, temporary scripts or test methods, manual database checks, regression probes — into maintained tests, e.g. replace an ad-hoc REST request with a `WebApplicationFactory` integration test. When an existing test already covers the behavior, verify that it really exercises it instead of adding a duplicate. Review temporary probes before promoting them to permanent tests.

## Smoke tests, coverage, snapshots

"Smoke test" means a small set of fast checks that a built or deployed application is basically operational — not a synonym for every integration test. Coverage is diagnostic, not a target; prioritize meaningful behavior, edge cases, and risky integrations. Snapshot testing can help for large stable outputs, but do not add a snapshot library by default; explicit assertions are clearer for small or important contracts.

## Anti-patterns

Avoid assertions that merely repeat the implementation, assertion-free tests (unless the behavior is "does not throw"), arbitrary delays such as `Task.Delay` to make timing-sensitive tests pass, and Testcontainers when no provider fidelity is required.

| Scenario | Default approach |
|---|---|
| Pure business rule | NUnit unit test with `[TestCase]` table |
| Application orchestration | Unit test with controlled boundary doubles when useful |
| Full API pipeline | `WebApplicationFactory<Program>` |
| Important persistence/provider behavior | Integration test against the actual provider |
| Time-dependent behavior | `TimeProvider` / `FakeTimeProvider` |
| External HTTP dependency | Stub handler or local fake server |
| Reproduced bug | Focused regression test |
| Temporary behavioral check | Convert to maintained coverage or confirm equivalent coverage |
| Deployment/basic health | Smoke test |
